coredata.dc:description: Two polyester polyurethane (PU)-degrading enzymes from Pseudomonaschlororaphis, a bacterium that utilizes polyester PU as the sole carbon and energy source,were purified to electrophoretic homogeneity as indicated by sodium dodecyl-polyacrylamide gelelectrophoresis (SDS–PAGE). Both enzymes are extracellular, soluble proteins with molecularweight of 63,000 Da and 31,000 Da. The 63,000 Da protein exhibits both esterase and proteaseactivities toward r-nitrophenylacetate and hide powder azure respectively. The enzyme has anoptimum pH of 8.5 for esterase activity and an optimum pH of 7.0 for protease activity. The31,000 Da protein exhibits esterase activity toward r-nitrophenylacetate, butyrate and propionate,and has an optimum pH of 8.5. In addition, the enzyme activities of both proteins are heat stableafter 10 min at 100°C and are inhibited 50% by the addition of 1 mMphenylmethylsulfonylfluoride indicating both are serine-hydrolases. © 1999 Elsevier Science Ltd.All rights reserved.

ce:section.ce:para: Polyurethanes (PUs) are a class of plastics which are widely used as raw materials in variousindustries. PUs are synthesized from polyols and polyisocyanates, and are classified into two types,polyester PUs and polyether PUs. Polyester PUs are considered to be comparatively susceptible tomicrobial degradation (Morton and Surman, 1994). Recycling of waste plastics has becomevery important because of shortages in raw materials for the synthesis of plastics. Due to theincompatibility of most polymers and the enormous difficulties encountered in segregating polymericarticles of different chemical composition found in plastic waste, complete recycling is difficult andlimited to special cases. Therefore, hydrolytic processes are being developed for the utilization ofplastic scrap and waste as either an energy source or as raw material for the production of valuablechemicals (Schnabel, 1981).

Despite its xenobiotic origins, PU has been found to be susceptible to biodegradation bynaturally occurring microorganisms (Pathiranar and Seal, 1984; Bentham et al., 1987,Bentham et al., 1988; Kay et al., 1991). Enzymatic attack on PUs could be contributed byhydrolases such as ureases, proteases and esterases (Evans and Levisohn, 1968; Hole, 1972; Flip, 1978; Griffin, 1980). Indeed, proteolytic enzymes (papain and urease)and cholesterol esterase have been shown to degrade PUs in vitro (Phua et al., 1987; Santerre et al., 1994).

Several reports have appeared in the literature on the susceptibility of PUs to fungal attack.Mechanisms for this susceptibility have been suggested by Darby and Kaplan (1968)and Kaplan et al. (1968), who have shown that polyester-type PUs are more susceptible to fungalattack than other forms. Four species of fungi, Curvularia sengalensis, Fusarium solani, Aureobasidium pullulans and Cladosporium sp. were isolated by Crabbe et al., 1994with the capability of degrading an ester-based PU (ImpranilTMDLN). Curvularia sengalensis was found to secrete an extracellular enzyme (molecularmass of 28 kDa) with esterase properties.

Recently, Nakajima-Kambe et al. (Nakajima-Kambe et al., 1995, Nakajima-Kambe et al., 1997) have reported a bacterial strain, Comamonas acidovorans,which will utilize solid polyester PU as the sole carbon and nitrogen source. These authors indicatedthe role of an extracellular membrane bound esterase activity in PU degradation. Purification of themembrane bound esterase revealed a thermally labile protein having a 62 kDa molecular mass. In aprevious report from this lab (Howard et al., 1998) stationary growth of Pseudomonaschlororaphis utilizing PU as the sole carbon and energy source was observed within 9 h in batchculture. The generation time for this bacterium was calculated to be 45 min. When the bacterium wasgrown on PU agar plates, zones of clearing were observed within 18 h. The enzymes from P.chlororaphis responsible for polyurethane degradation were found to be extracellular.Zymogram analysis of the extracellular soluble proteins from P. chlororaphis usingnon-denaturing polyacrylamide gels revealed three PUase active protein bands with R f values of 0.25, 0.417 and 0.917. The present study describes the purification andcharacterization of two PUase enzymes from P. chlororaphis which corresponds with theR f values 0.25 and 0.917, as previously described from cultural supernants of P. chlororaphis.

Pseudomonas chlororaphis was isolated from a microbial consortium obtained fromthe Naval Research Laboratory, Washington, DC by its ability to degrade a water dispersiblepolyurethane. Pseudomonas chlororaphis was grown at 30°C with constant shaking on theyeast extract salts (YES) medium previously described by Crabbe et al., 1994.

A 3 l culture of P. chlororaphis was incubated for three days in YES mediasupplemented with Impranil (Bayer Corp.) at a final concentration of 3.0 g l−1. At theend of three days of incubation, little visible Impranil remained and the culture solids were removedby centrifugation at 10,000×g for 20 min at 4°C. All remaining manipulations wereconducted at 4°C. The supernatant from the cell free extract was clarified by tangential flow highperformance ultrafiltration (HPUF) using a 0.3 micron membrane to remove residual polyurethaneand cell debris. The clarified filtrate was passed over a 5×7 cm column of DEAE–cellulose which hadbeen previously equilibrated in 50 mM phosphate buffer at pH 7.0 at a flow rate of ∼250 ml h−1. The non-binding fraction was either used immediately for kinetics studies orconcentrated by membrane filtration on a 10 kDa molecular weight cutoff membrane (Amicon) andused without further purification.

After each stage of the purification process, the purity of the enzyme was assessed bypolyacrylamide gel electrophoresis (PAGE). Non-denaturing (ND) gels were run with a 12%polyacrylamide resolving gel as described by Calza et al. (1985). Sodium dodecyl sulfate (SDS)–PAGE was performed as described by Laemmli (1970)with a 12% polyacrylamideresolving gel. Proteins were visualized by Coomassie blue (Sigma) staining.

During the purification, aliquots of the protein fractions were spotted on YES agar platessupplemented with Impranil at pH 6.8 and examined for zones of clearing at 30°C. Assays todetermine the proteolytic activity of the enzyme used hide powder azure (Calbiochem) in 50 mMphosphate buffer at pH 6.8 (Chavira et al., 1984). Activity against hide powder azure wasdetermined by monitoring the increase in absorbance at 595 nm. One unit of activity was defined asthe amount of enzyme that changes the absorbance at 595 nm by 0.01 min−1. Inaddition, the enzyme was assayed for esterase activity by its ability to release r-nitrophenol from 8 mM r-nitrophenolacetate in 50 mM phosphate buffer, pH 6.8 at 30°C (Deshpande et al., 1984). One unit of esterase activity was defined as the amount of enzyme that produced 1 mmoleof r-nitrophenol per minute. All enzyme assays were observed to be linear with respect to time andprotein concentration under the tested conditions.

Impranil zymograms were carried out by using a ND–PAGE gel overlaid on a 0.7% (w/v)agarose gel containing 0.1% (v/v) Impranil in 50 mM phosphate buffer, pH 6.8. The zymogram wasincubated for 12 to 18 hr at 30°C. The polyacrylamide gel was removed and the agarose gel wasflooded with a 0.1% (w/v) Coomassie blue R-250 solution in 40% (v/v) methanol and 10% (v/v)acetic acid for 20 min. The Coomassie blue solution was then poured off and the plates flooded with40% (v/v) methanol and 10% (v/v) acetic acid for 20 min. Visualized clear zones of degradationwere observed in a blue background.
Protein concentrations were estimated by the methods of either Kalb and Bernlohr (1977)or Bradford (1976).

A summary of the purification of the two polyurethanase proteins from P. chlororaphis is described in Table 1 . Protein concentrations were estimated by the method of Kalb and Bernlohr (1977), sincethe concentration of proteins was under the lower limits of sensitivity for the method of Bradford (1976)to detect. The steps of the purification were completed in <10 h. Three PUaseproteins were eluted from the anion exchange column using a step-wise NaCl gradient (0 to 1.0 M).

The first PUase enzyme was recovered in the run through volume with no addition of NaCland resulted in 33.3% recovery of enzymatic activity in the crude extract. The extracellular solublePUase protein was purified to apparent electrophoretic homogeneity as indicated by the appearanceof a single band on ND–PAGE gels [Fig. 1 (A)]. The appearance of a single zone of clearing on the PU zymogram which corresponded to thesingle band on the ND–PAGE gel indicates that this protein is involved in the degradation of PU [Fig. 1 (B)]. A plot of log MW versus R f for the SDS–PAGE gelindicate a single 63 kDa protein (Fig. 2 ).

The catalytic properties of the first purified PUase protein obtained from the run throughfraction of the anion exchange column revealed both protease and esterase activities. Usingr-nitrophenylacetate as the esterase substrate, the purified protein displayed a specific activity of 8.5 U mg−1 and a steady state kinetic parameter of 12 mM for K m. Theoptimum pH was determined to be 8.4 and the enzyme activity was stable after 10 min at 100°C. Theesterase activity was inhibited 50% by the addition of 1 mM PMSF. When hide powder azure wasused as the protease substrate, the purified protein displayed a specific activity of 3.33 U mg−1 and an optimum pH of 7.0.

The catalytic properties of the purified PUase protein obtained from the 0.1 M NaCl fractionof the anion exchange column revealed only an esterase activity. Using r-nitrophenylacetate as theesterase substrate, the purified protein displayed a specific activity of 19.9 U mg−1. Inaddition, the enzyme exhibited activity against rnitrophenylpropionate, 11.6 U mg−1and r-nitrophenylbutyrate, 3.6 U mg−1. The optimum pH for the enzyme activitytowards r-nitrophenylacetate was determined to be higher than 8.5 (38.7 U mg−1).Unfortunately, the background hydrolysis rate at this pH and higher was too high to obtain accuratemeasurements. The enzyme activity was stable after 10 min at 100°C and the esterase activity wasinhibited 50% by the addition of 1 mM PMSF. When hide powder azure was used as the proteasesubstrate, the purified protein displayed no activity against this substrate, indicating that the enzymeexhibited only esterase activity and displayed no protease activity.

In a previous study by this lab, the cell-free supernatant of P. chlororaphis wasshown to contain three distinct PUase activities as revealed by ND–PAGE zymograms (Howard et al., 1998). Two of the three enzyme activities have been accounted for by proteinpurification. The purification of the slow migrating PUase, R f 0.25, revealed apolypeptide with a molecular mass of 63 kDa, displaying both protease and esterase activity (thisstudy). The molecular mass of this protein is similar to the PUase purified from C. acidovorans, 62 kDa, (Akutsu et al., 1998). The faster migrating PUase, R f0.917, (this study), was shown to exhibit a molecular mass of 31 kDa. The molecular mass of thisprotein is similar to the PUase proteins purified from Curvularia sengalensis, 28 kDa (Crabbe et al., 1994) and P. fluorescens, 29 kDa (Howard and Blake, 1998).

Hole, 1972hypothesized enzymatic attack on polyurethanes could include proteasesattacking the amide and urethane bonds, esterases hydrolyzing the many ester bonds and ureasesattacking the urea units. Indeed, proteolytic enzymes (papain and urease) and cholesterol esterasehave been shown to degrade polyurethanes in vitro (Phua et al., 1987; Santerre et al., 1994). The 63 kDa PUase protein purified in this study displayed both esterase andprotease activities. Protease activity was also shown in the PUase purified from P. fluorescens (Howard and Blake, 1998), but no esterase activity was detected in this study. Theesterase activity is in agreement with other purified PUases (Akutsu et al., 1998; Crabbe et al., 1994), however, these purified PUase displayed no protease activity. Interestingly, allthe PUase enzymes described thus far are inhibited by PMSF, indicating that these proteins which areinvolved in PU degradation are serine-hydrolases. Future work is underway with the purified PUasefrom P. chlororaphis to determine the PU degradation pathway along with screening thegenomic libraries already constructed from P. chlororaphis.
